segments.title: Why school history is necessarily selective
segments.summary: A school history course must reduce large subjects to teachable pieces, even when its teachers know the subject well.
segments.body: The objection to the phrase "this is what I was taught at school" is not an attack on teachers or school history. Teachers have limited time and budgets, while history competes with every other school subject. A course has to make difficult material manageable by selecting a small number of points. The BBC's "Bitesize" label provides a useful analogy: pupils receive an intelligible portion rather than every connected detail. Trouble begins when that introductory account is treated as the whole of history.

evidence.note: He distinguishes classroom time limits from the quality of history teachers and compares school material to bite-sized learning.

segments.title: War aims and factions within states
segments.summary: Before World War I, factions within the same country could press for war while others resisted it, which makes a state difficult to treat as a single actor.
segments.body: Accounts of the route to World War I often say that particular powers wanted war, but that shorthand can hide disagreement inside each state. Some factions sought conflict while others strongly opposed it. A contributing factor may also affect different strategic relationships in different ways. Historians therefore need to separate a state's broad course from the competing intentions inside it. The Berlin-Baghdad railway example makes that causal complexity concrete.

evidence.note: He contrasts factions within the same states that wanted war with factions that strongly opposed conflict, then cautions that contributing factors do not all operate in one direction.

segments.title: The Berlin-Baghdad railway and competing interests
segments.summary: A World War I example shows why a single factor can trouble one power while also serving another of its strategic interests.
segments.body: The Berlin-Baghdad railway shows how the same development could pull British policy in opposite directions. The railway could alarm Britain because it threatened its eastern holdings, yet a stronger Ottoman Empire could help contain Russia. Following that second line opens a much larger explanation involving Anglo-Russian tensions over India and the Far East, along with the consequences of the Russo-Japanese War. A classroom survey may present only the first side because explaining both takes far more time. The familiar account remains useful, but it becomes more accurate when these conflicting interests are kept in view.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the railway's threat to British eastern holdings with its value in strengthening the Ottoman Empire against Russia, then names the wider context needed.

segments.title: History as lifelong study
segments.summary: School provides a foundation, but understanding historical causes more fully requires continued reading beyond examinations.
segments.body: School history can be sound while necessarily incomplete. Examinations impose a practical limit on how far any course can go, and the same selectivity can affect university teaching. Historical understanding grows when people continue studying after the required syllabus ends and follow the connections behind a familiar account. Passion and continued study matter to good historical teaching as well as good historical practice. Classroom time limits therefore explain why learning history remains a lifelong pursuit.

evidence.note: He says history is a lifelong pursuit and explains that school lacks time to present the full picture.
